The notebooks below accompany Unit 3. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots); open
them in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment.

## Shortest paths in graphs

The starting point for the unit: a weighted graph is described by its
weighted adjacency matrix $W$, with $W_{ij}$ the cost of moving from node
$i$ to node $j$ and $\infty$ meaning no edge (the matrix is symmetric for
an undirected graph, and need not be for a directed one). The notebook
solves the same six-node example three different ways, so the algorithms
of the notes can be compared side by side on a problem small enough to
check by hand.

[Download `A_3_shortestpathgraphs.ipynb`](A_3_shortestpathgraphs.ipynb){download="A_3_shortestpathgraphs.ipynb"}

## Robot path planning on a grid

The deterministic robot-planning example: an environment divided into
cells, where moving to a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell costs
$1$ and a diagonal move costs $\sqrt2$, obstacle cells are at infinite
distance, and so is a diagonal move that would squeeze between two cells
adjacent to the same obstacle. The dynamic programming algorithm computes
the optimal policy, and the shortest path from A to B is then read off by
following the arrows. The obstacle matrix `M` is easy to edit, so it is
worth re-running on an environment of your own.

[Download `A_3_RobotPlanningDeterministic.ipynb`](A_3_RobotPlanningDeterministic.ipynb){download="A_3_RobotPlanningDeterministic.ipynb"}

## Shortest-path policy in Pac-Man's grid world

Pac-Man as a pursuit-evasion game on a grid of 77 cells, where a ghost
chases Pac-Man and both may move to an adjacent cell or stay put. Here
Pac-Man is *stationary*, so the ghost's task is simply to take the first
step of a shortest path from its own cell to Pac-Man's -- shortest in
both time and cells travelled -- with ties broken by the smallest cell
label. A direct application of the shortest-path machinery to a state
space that is a real map rather than an abstract graph.

[Download `A_3_A_Shortest_path_policy_pacman.ipynb`](A_3_A_Shortest_path_policy_pacman.ipynb){download="A_3_A_Shortest_path_policy_pacman.ipynb"}

## Intersection policy in Pac-Man's grid world

The same grid world, but now Pac-Man *moves*, along a path that is
periodic and known in advance. Chasing the cell Pac-Man currently
occupies is no longer right: the ghost should head for a cell where the
two will meet, so as to intersect Pac-Man in the fewest iterations. The
comparison with the previous notebook is the point -- the same map and
the same algorithms, but a target that has to be predicted rather than
merely located.

[Download `A_3_A_Intersection_policy_pacman.ipynb`](A_3_A_Intersection_policy_pacman.ipynb){download="A_3_A_Intersection_policy_pacman.ipynb"}

## The 8-puzzle on a torus

The classic sliding-tile puzzle, solved with both Dijkstra's algorithm
and A\*. The variant used here removes the boundary, so the frame wraps
around and there are always exactly four possible moves rather than the
two or three available at an edge or corner in the usual game. It is the
best illustration in the unit of a state space that is enormous yet
perfectly well defined -- every reachable tile arrangement is a node --
and therefore of why a good heuristic matters.

[Download `A_3_K_Puzzle8.ipynb`](A_3_K_Puzzle8.ipynb){download="A_3_K_Puzzle8.ipynb"}
